procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of acquittal of the appellants under s. 23(1A) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court at Calcutta set aside the order of acquittal and convicted the appellants under s. 23(1A) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeals were filed in the Supreme Court by special leave against the judgment of the High Court. The Supreme Court initially delivered a judgment on August 18, 1970, upholding the High Court's conviction. Subsequently, a review petition was filed, and a further judgment was delivered on February 18, 1971, partly allowing the review petition and modifying the sentence of one of the appellants.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal of Puranmall Jain is allowed. The appeals of Girdhari Lal and Bhagwandeo Tewari are dismissed. The review petition is partly allowed.
decision.conviction_status: Puranmall Jain is acquitted of the charge.
decision.sentence_status: The sentence of six months' rigorous imprisonment imposed on Girdharilal is set aside. The sentence of fine of Rs. 2,000/- shall, however, stand.
directions: His bail bond shall stand cancelled.

issue.issue_text: The evidence of an investigating officer who conducts a search cannot be relied on unless it is corroborated.

facts: An investigating officer (C. R. Basu, P.W. 6) conducted a search of a premises and testified about the documents he seized, including account books and three account slips.
The appellants argued that the officer's evidence could not be relied upon without corroboration.
Another witness (P.W. 8, Lalit C. L. Parekh) was present at the search and signed the search document.
The entries in the seized account slips were found to tally with entries in the seized account books.
law: The Supreme Court held that the proposition that an investigating officer's evidence must be corroborated to be reliable is a "novel one" with no supporting principle or authority.
The Court established that the reliability of an investigating officer's testimony is not a matter of a fixed legal rule, but rather "depends on the facts in each case."
application: The Court directly addressed the appellant's argument, stating it was a "novel proposition" for which no legal authority or principle could be cited.
Instead of a rigid rule requiring corroboration, the Court determined that the credibility of the officer's testimony should be assessed based on the specific circumstances of the case.

The Court then pointed out that, even if corroboration were required, it existed in this case. The officer's testimony was corroborated by the evidence of P.W. 8, who signed the search document, and by the physical evidence of the account books, whose entries tallied with the seized slips.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that there is no general rule of law that the evidence of an investigating officer who conducts a search must be corroborated. The Court found that the credibility of such evidence depends on the facts of each case and noted that, in this specific instance, there was sufficient corroborating evidence anyway.

issue.issue_text: The account slips discovered during the search could not be taken into consideration because they were not evidence.

facts: Account slips were discovered and seized during a search of the premises.
The defense counsel argued that these slips could not be considered because they were not evidence.
The defense also suggested that the slips had been fabricated and planted by the investigating officer.
The entries on the seized slips were found to have been carried over into the firm's account books.
law: Items discovered during a search are considered part of the evidence.
There is no general principle of law that an investigating officer's evidence about a search cannot be relied on unless it is corroborated.
application: The Court stated it was "unable to appreciate" why the slips were not evidence, finding the argument to have "no substance."
The Court reasoned that since the slips were part of the items discovered during the search, they were admissible.
Crucially, the Court pointed out that the entries on the slips corresponded with entries in the firm's account books.
This correspondence served two purposes: it provided a strong reason to consider the slips as evidence, and it demolished the defense's claim that the slips were fabricated.
The Court also dismissed the fabrication claim because the defense had not questioned the witnesses about it during the trial, and the court would not presume an officer would fabricate evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the account slips were valid evidence and could be taken into consideration. The Court reasoned that they were discovered during the search and, more importantly, their authenticity was corroborated by the fact that the entries on them matched the entries in the firm's own account books.

issue.issue_text: The account slips were fabricated and planted as they were not mentioned separately in the search list and there is no evidence of when the sealed parcel containing them was opened.

facts: The defense argued that certain account slips were fabricated and planted by the investigating officer.
The basis for this argument was that the search list did not mention the slips separately, but only referred to "loose sheets in a sealed parcel."
The defense also pointed out that there was no evidence showing when the sealed parcel was opened.
Crucially, entries found on the seized slips were also found to have been carried over into the firm's official account books.
law: The court will not presume that an investigating officer has fabricated evidence without any proof.
Items discovered during a search are considered evidence.
The failure of the defense to question witnesses (specifically the investigating officer) about an allegation of fabrication during the trial weakens that argument on appeal.
application: The Court dismissed the fabrication argument as a mere suggestion, noting that the defense never questioned the witnesses or the investigating officer about this specific allegation during the trial.
The Court refused to presume that the investigating officer would fabricate evidence simply to incriminate the appellants.

Most importantly, the Court found that the defense's claim was directly contradicted by the evidence. The fact that entries from the disputed slips were also present in the firm's own account books served as powerful corroboration that the slips were genuine and belonged to the firm.
The Court also noted that a witness to the search had signed the search list and testified that slips of paper were seized, further corroborating the investigating officer's evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the claim of fabrication was an unsubstantiated suggestion. The Court found compelling evidence of the slips' authenticity because the entries on them matched entries in the firm's own account books, which effectively demolished the defense's case on this issue.

issue.issue_text: The case was fit for review because the court's attention was not drawn to a relevant statutory provision (sub-s. 23C(2)) during the original arguments.

facts: A review petition was filed by Girdharilal Gupta on the grounds that his counsel had omitted to bring section 23C(2) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act to the court's attention during the original appeal.
The petitioner argued that this specific provision had a "vital bearing on the case."
The counsel for the State argued against the review, claiming it was not a fit case for review but merely a "case of mistaken judgment."
application: The Supreme Court explicitly disagreed with the State's argument that the case was not fit for review.
The Court acknowledged that its attention had not been specifically drawn to section 23C(2) and the "light it throws on the interpretation of sub-s. (1)" during the initial arguments.
Based on this omission, the Court decided to re-open the judgment from the original criminal appeal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that the case was fit for review. It rejected the State's objection and agreed with the petitioner that the failure to consider the relevant statutory provision, section 23C(2), during the original arguments was a sufficient reason to re-examine the case.

issue.issue_text: An officer of a company, such as a manager, may not be in overall charge of the business and may only be in charge of a part of it, which affects their liability.

law.fact: Section 23C(1) of the relevant Act imposes vicarious liability on "every person who, at the time the contravention was committed, was in-charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company."
law.reasoning: The Court noted that this is a highly penal section and must be construed strictly.

law.fact: Section 23C(2) provides for liability for other officers, such as directors, if the offense was committed with their consent, connivance, or due to their neglect.
law.reasoning: The Court used the structure of this subsection to infer the meaning of "in-charge" in the first subsection.

application.fact: The Court interpreted the phrase "a person in-charge" under Section 23C(1) to mean the person who is in "overall control of the day to day business of the company or firm."
application.reasoning: This interpretation was derived from the context provided by Section 23C(2). The Court reasoned that Section 23C(2) mentions directors who might set policy but not be involved in day-to-day business, and managers who might be in charge of the business but not in *overall* charge.

application.fact: The Court explicitly distinguished between different levels of responsibility within a company.
application.reasoning: It stated that some directors may only lay down policy and not be concerned with daily operations. Similarly, other officers, including a manager, might only be in charge of a specific part of the company's business. These individuals would not meet the standard of being in "overall control."

application.fact: The Court cited a similar case, State v. S. P. Bhadani, which interpreted a comparable law.
application.reasoning: In that case, it was held that liability was confined to officers in the "immediate charge of the management of the company," and that officers not in direct charge were immune unless they consented to or connived in the offense.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the distinction, holding that for an officer to be vicariously liable under Section 23C(1), they must be in 'overall control of the day to day business.' The Court reasoned that other officers, such as a manager or director, who are only responsible for a part of the business or for setting policy, do not meet this standard and are therefore not automatically liable for the company's offenses.

arguments.issue_text: The evidence of an investigating officer who conducts a search cannot be relied on unless it is corroborated.
appellant_arguments: The evidence of the investigating officer is unreliable and should not be accepted without corroboration, implying that the officer may have fabricated evidence like the account slips.
respondent_arguments: The investigating officer's testimony is credible on its own, and there is no reason to presume that an officer would fabricate evidence to incriminate the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: The account slips discovered during the search could not be taken into consideration because they were not evidence.
appellant_arguments: The account slips found during the search should be disregarded entirely because they do not constitute evidence.
respondent_arguments: The slips are valid evidence as they were discovered during the search, and the entries on them were subsequently transferred to the firm's account books.

arguments.issue_text: The account slips were fabricated and planted as they were not mentioned separately in the search list and there is no evidence of when the sealed parcel containing them was opened.
appellant_arguments: The account slips were fabricated after the search, which is proven by the fact that they do not bear the signature of the witness who signed the other seized documents.
respondent_arguments: The claim of fabrication is baseless. The witness signed numerous documents and could have simply forgotten to sign these specific slips. Furthermore, the entries from the slips are reflected in the firm's account books, which demolishes the fabrication theory.

arguments.issue_text: The case was fit for review because the court's attention was not drawn to a relevant statutory provision (sub-s. 23C(2)) during the original arguments.
appellant_arguments: The case is suitable for review because a key statutory provision was overlooked during the initial arguments.
respondent_arguments: The case is not fit for review because the original decision was simply a case of mistaken judgment, not a fundamental error.

arguments.issue_text: An officer of a company, such as a manager, may not be in overall charge of the business and may only be in charge of a part of it, which affects their liability.
appellant_arguments: To be held liable, the prosecution must prove that the person was in charge of the conduct of the business, and the evidence presented was insufficient to establish this.
respondent_arguments: The appellant was in charge of the business, as evidenced by his own statement that he 'alone looked after the affairs of the firm', making him liable under the statute.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A person 'in-charge' of a company or firm must be in overall control of the day-to-day business. There is no legal principle that requires the evidence of an investigating officer who conducts a search to be corroborated, as its reliability depends on the facts of each case. Items discovered during a search are considered evidence.
obiter: A case is fit for review if the court's attention was not drawn to a statutory sub-section that sheds light on the interpretation of another.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found the evidence of the investigating officer to be credible and the account slips discovered during the search to be valid, admissible evidence. The argument that these slips were fabricated was rejected because the entries from the slips were subsequently carried into the firm's official account books, which demolished the defense's theory. However, the court accepted that the case was fit for review on a point of law regarding vicarious liability, ultimately holding that to be 'in-charge' under s. 23C(1), a person must be in overall control of the day-to-day business, a standard which was not met for one of the appellants.
legal_tests_applied: In the context of s. 23C(l), a person 'in-charge' must mean that the person should be in over all control of the day to day business of the company or firm. This inference follows from the wording of s. 23C(2), which distinguishes between officers like directors or managers who may be in charge of only some part of the business and not in overall charge.
why_appellant_lost: The court found the evidence of the investigating officer impressive and saw no reason not to place reliance on it, refusing to presume that the officer would fabricate evidence.

The court rejected the argument that the account slips were not evidence, stating, 'We are unable to appreciate why they are not evidence. These are part of the things discovered during search and if the entries therein are carried into the account books there is no reason why these things could not be looked at.'

The claim that the account slips were fabricated was dismissed because 'the entries in the account books demolish the case of defence that these slips were fabricated and that they had nothing to do with the firm.'
why_respondent_won: The case was deemed fit for review because 'at the time of arguments the attention of the court was not drawn specifically to sub-s. 23C(2) and the light it throws on the interpretation of sub-s.(1)'. The court rejected the respondent's argument that this was merely a case of mistaken judgment.

The court accepted that an officer of a company, such as a manager, may not be in overall charge of the business but only a part of it, which affects liability under the statute. It reasoned that s. 23C(2) mentions officers like a director or manager who may not be in overall charge of the business.
policy_considerations: When a person is being vicariously punished for a contravention that occurred while they were abroad, making it possible it happened without their knowledge or lack of diligence, a sentence of imprisonment may not be appropriate; a fine would better meet the ends of justice.
